Carthage

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Carthage
FoundedTraditionally 814 BC, by settlers from Tyre
LocationGulf of Tunis, present-day Tunisia
GovernmentMonarchy, later republic ruled by suffetes and a senate
Destroyed146 BC by Rome (Third Punic War); later refounded as a Roman city
Notable figuresHannibal Barca, Hamilcar Barca, Dido (legendary founder)

Carthage was an ancient city in Northern Africa, on the eastern side of Lake Tunis in what is now Tunisia. It was founded by Phoenician colonists from Tyre — traditionally in 814 BC — and grew into the dominant power of the western Mediterranean, a wealthy commercial empire whose trading network reached from Iberia to the Levant.

History

Carthage established colonies and trading posts across North Africa, Sardinia, Corsica, Ibiza, and western Sicily. Its wealth rested on maritime trade, agriculture in the fertile Tunisian interior, and the famous purple dye industry. Conflict with the Greek cities of Sicily ran for centuries before Rome emerged as Carthage's great rival.

Punic Wars

Rome and Carthage fought three Punic Wars (264–241, 218–201, and 149–146 BC). In the second, the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants and won a devastating victory at Cannae (216 BC), but Rome ultimately prevailed under Scipio Africanus at Zama (202 BC). In 146 BC, after a three-year siege, Rome destroyed the city and annexed its territory. Augustus later refounded Carthage as a Roman colony, and it became one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire.

Society and religion

Carthaginian society was headed by wealthy merchant families; the government, praised by Aristotle, mixed elected magistrates (suffetes), a senate, and popular assemblies. Religion centred on deities such as Baal Hammon and Tanit. The tophet precinct, containing urns of cremated infants, has long been debated as evidence for or against child sacrifice.
